packets.key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay-minimum option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, because nudged cardholders set autopay only slightly above the minimum and reduced manual payments.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on live UK credit card accounts with a 6-month follow-up.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly shows a default-style nudge can shift a nominal enrollment/behavior metric without changing the real financial outcome — exactly the vanity-enrollment risk the support team raised for round-up defaults, and unlike most of this literature it studies a genuine consumer financial product rather than an employer plan.
limitations: credit card debt repayment, not a savings product
the mechanism is shrouding a minimum-payment option, not an enrollment default per se
packets.relevance_reason: Closest available consumer-product evidence that a default-style nudge can raise a compliance metric without improving the substantive outcome, directly bearing on the brief's central 'vanity enrollment' question.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges shift risk-taking by medium-to-large effect sizes but also lower consumers' rating of the advice delivered, especially when the default is one they refuse.
packets.methodology: Three experiments; the largest uses representative samples across five European countries.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the reputational/manipulation cost of a default in a European consumer financial-advice context — exactly the dark-pattern risk the brief flags for the entry design decision — and shows framing of the default question itself changes outcomes.
limitations: wealth-management risk allocation, not a round-up savings multiplier
no long-term follow-up on retention or amount saved
packets.relevance_reason: EU consumer-financial evidence, with effect sizes, on when a default is perceived as manipulative rather than helpful — central to the brief's dark-pattern concern.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for when default effects persist or fade downstream, identifying time course, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators.
packets.methodology: Conceptual review and research-agenda paper synthesizing prior default-effect literature, abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Provides the conceptual vocabulary for the exact question the team needs answered — whether the round-up default's effect on enrollment will persist or decay, and for whom — framed at the level of general consumer decision-making rather than employer plans.
limitations: conceptual synthesis, not new empirical effect sizes
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: Supplies the general framework for predicting persistence and heterogeneity of default effects that the brief's core trade-off depends on.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: Adding a minor enrollment 'ordeal' (extra step) to a health-insurance auto-enrollment policy reduced enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged individuals.
packets.methodology: Natural experiment studying the removal/addition of an auto-enrollment step in a public health-insurance selection market, with a theoretical adverse-selection model.
packets.why_it_matters: Shows that adding friction (moving away from opt-out toward active choice/opt-in) has large, distributionally uneven effects on who stays enrolled, directly bearing on who is helped versus hurt by our entry-design choice.
limitations: Health-insurance selection market, not a consumer financial savings product
Adverse-selection framing does not map cleanly onto a savings feature with no insurance risk pooling
packets.relevance_reason: Strongest available distributional evidence on the enrolment cost of adding friction, bearing directly on who is hurt by moving away from opt-out.
packets.title: Do Ordeals Work for Selection Markets? Evidence from Health Insurance Auto-Enrollment
packets.abstract: Are application hassles, or “ordeals,” an effective way to limit public program enrollment? We provide new evidence by studying (removal of) an auto-enrollment policy for health insurance, adding an extra step to enroll. This minor ordeal has a major impact, reducing enrollment by 33 percent and differentially excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people. Using a simple model, we show adverse selection—a classic feature of insurance markets—undermines ordeals’ standard rationale of excluding low-value individuals since they are also low-cost and may not be inefficient. Our analysis illustrates why ordeals targeting is unlikely to work well in selection markets. (JEL D82, G22, H75, I13, I18)

packets.key_finding: Switching university exam sign-up to opt-out increased sign-ups, but effortful downstream completion (exam participation and passing) improved only for previously 'responsive' students, with no effect for non-responsive individuals.
packets.methodology: Two field experiments changing exam sign-up defaults to opt-out at a university, tracking downstream effortful task completion.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the mechanism the support team worries about: a default can inflate nominal sign-up while doing nothing for engagement among people who were not going to act anyway, precisely the 'vanity enrollment' risk for round-up savings.
limitations: University exam sign-up, not a financial savings decision
No amount-saved or 6-12 month withdrawal data given
packets.relevance_reason: Best available evidence that opt-out defaults can inflate nominal participation without changing effortful downstream behavior for disengaged users, the core mechanism behind the brief's vanity-enrolment worry.
packets.title: Defaults and effortful tasks
packets.abstract: Abstract Nothing is known about the effectiveness of defaults when moving the target outcomes requires substantial effort. We conduct two field experiments to investigate how defaults fare in such situations: we change the university exam sign-up procedure in two study programs to “opt-out” (a) for a single exam, and (b) for many exams. Both interventions increase task uptake (exam sign-up). Concerning the outcomes which require effort, we find no effects for many exams. For a single exam, the opt-out increases task completion (exam participation) in the study program where the default arguably entails stronger endorsement. Within this program, the effects on successful task completion (exam passing) are heterogeneous: treated students who in the past were willing to communicate with the university (responsive individuals) invest more effort into exam preparation and are more likely to pass the exam than their control counterparts.For non-responsive individuals, we find increased sign-ups but no effects on the target outcomes. Defaults can thus be effective and may be an attractive policy option even when the target outcome requires substantial effort provision. It is, however crucial that the interventions target the appropriate individuals.

packets.key_finding: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans finds automatic enrollment raises steady-state saving rates by only 0.6% of income and auto-escalation defaults by only 0.3%, and only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on the first date, with more opting out later.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal administrative-data analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation and balance-withdrawal dynamics.
packets.why_it_matters: The strongest recent quantitative evidence that headline default 'take-up' overstates the real medium/long-run effect on amounts saved — precisely the vanity-enrollment risk the support team raises for round-up defaults.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated auto-escalation, no direct fintech app analogue
packets.relevance_reason: Directly contradicts the 'defaults always help' premise with real numbers on how much smaller the effect is once medium/long-run dynamics are accounted for.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: Automatic enrollment into just-in-time SMS overdraft alerts at major UK banks reduced unarranged overdraft charges by 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges by 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in annual market-wide savings, though users still captured less than half of the achievable savings.
packets.methodology: At-scale randomized field experiments run with major UK retail banks on an existing consumer banking app feature.
packets.why_it_matters: This is the closest available evidence to our own decision: automatic enrolment into a consumer banking app feature with quantified effect sizes, plus evidence that even a successful default leaves much of the potential benefit unrealized, directly bearing on enrolment vs. amount-saved.
limitations: Overdraft alerts, not a savings/contribution feature, so 'amount saved' logic differs from round-up mechanics
No 6-12 month persistence data given beyond the trial window
packets.relevance_reason: Closest prior work: consumer retail-bank automatic-enrolment field experiments with quantified effect sizes in the exact UK/EU regulatory and market context.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults raised donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with disproportionately larger effects on smaller, first-time donors who likely did not intend the recurring commitment.
packets.methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design exploiting the different timing of default rollout across political-campaign donation websites.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates the support team's concern in a real setting: defaults on recurring financial commitments raise uptake but generate disproportionate refunds/complaints among naive users, the exact 'vanity enrollment' risk named in the brief.
limitations: Political donations, not a savings or banking product
No 6-12 month retention data beyond refund requests
packets.relevance_reason: Closest empirical demonstration of a default-induced recurring financial commitment causing complaint/refund behavior concentrated among less-experienced users, mirroring the support team's objection.
packets.title: Dark defaults: How choice architecture steers political campaign donations
packets.abstract: In the months before the 2020 U.S. election, several political campaign websites added prechecked boxes (defaults), automatically making all donations into recurring weekly contributions unless donors unchecked them. Since these changes occurred at different times for different campaigns, we use a staggered difference-in-differences design to measure the causal effects of defaults on donors' behavior. We estimate that defaults increased campaign donations by over $43 million while increasing requested refunds by almost $3 million. The weekly default only impacted weekly recurring donations, and not other donations, suggesting that donors may not have intended to make weekly donations. The longer defaults were displayed, the more money campaigns raised through weekly donations. Donors did not compensate by changing the amount they donated. We found that the default had a larger impact on smaller donors and on donors who had no prior experience with defaults, causing them to start more chains and donate a larger proportion of their money through weekly recurring donations.
packets.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

packets.key_finding: Across three large firms, automatic enrolment raised 401(k) participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the default savings rate (2-3%) and default fund, and half still remained at the default rate and fund after three years; automatic enrolment increased saving mainly in the lower tail of the distribution.
packets.methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large U.S. firms comparing pre- and post-automatic-enrolment cohorts.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantitative evidence that a pre-set contribution level anchors most people for years, directly bearing on decision 2 (whether a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor users away from a higher level they might otherwise choose) and on whether the enrolment lift is a net saving-amount gain or just a nominal one.
limitations: employer-sponsored 401(k) setting rather than a self-directed consumer app
three-firm sample, U.S. retirement context
packets.relevance_reason: Closest available quantitative evidence on anchoring at a pre-set default level and its persistence over years, central to the level/multiplier decision.
packets.title: For Better or For Worse: Default Effects and 401(k) Savings Behavior
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan. Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation. We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so. As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle. We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund). Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund. The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward. While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation. In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average. However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

packets.key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic (passive) retirement contributions raised wealth accumulation substantially, while active-choice tax subsidies induced mostly asset-shifting (each $1 of subsidy raised total saving by only 1 cent); ~85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but strongly moved by automatic contributions, and active savers are wealthier and more sophisticated.
packets.methodology: Population-scale administrative panel data analysis of Danish savings and retirement account activity.
packets.why_it_matters: The strongest available quantification of how much more effective passive/automatic mechanisms are than active-choice incentives, and of who the passive-responders are, directly informing the brief's 'who is helped, who is hurt' question and the credibility of the defaults-lift-enrolment premise.
limitations: Danish retirement/pension accounts, employer-linked, not a self-directed liquid consumer app
subsidy-based active choice differs from an active-choice onboarding screen
packets.relevance_reason: Closest and strongest available evidence quantifying the size and distributional heterogeneity of default versus active-choice effects on saving, a necessary reference point even though the setting is retirement accounts.
packets.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
packets.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.

alternates.key_finding: Active-choice policies (requiring an explicit yes/no) are an effective alternative to opt-out defaults where opt-out is infeasible or unethical, and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option outperforms plain active choice in field experiments.
alternates.methodology: Literature review plus a series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and enhanced active choice against no-default and opt-out conditions.
alternates.why_it_matters: The closest existing evidence directly comparing active choice against opt-out defaults, the central question behind the brief's decision on whether forced choice can capture most of the enrolment benefit without the disengagement cost.
limitations: applications drawn mainly from health/medication adherence and retirement contexts, not a fintech app
abstract gives no numeric enrolment effect sizes
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly targets the active-choice-versus-default comparison (C6) that decision 1 turns on, proposing a specific enhanced design the team could test.
alternates.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
alternates.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: A randomized reminder-nudge intervention in a consumer credit card app cut late-payment fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9%, with users who had a history of overdraft use experiencing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
alternates.methodology: Field experiment (RCT) with a financial management platform in Brazil, comparing users randomized to receive payment reminders versus not, tracking downstream fee outcomes across credit card and checking accounts.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives a quantified, real consumer-fintech demonstration that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup — directly bears on the brief's requirement to check who is hurt, not just average enrolment lift, before defaulting everyone into round-ups.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
Brazilian credit/overdraft market, not EU round-up savings context
does not measure enrolment or persistence in a savings feature
alternates.relevance_reason: Closest available empirical evidence on heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, effects of a consumer financial nudge — speaks directly to the brief's distributional/manipulation-risk concern (C5) and to the 'one size fits all' caution against blanket opt-out defaults.
alternates.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
alternates.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

alternates.key_finding: A synthesis of household-finance behaviour covering consumption/saving, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, and of interventions (education, peer effects, product design, choice architecture, disclosure) that firms and governments use to shape financial outcomes.
alternates.methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter synthesizing empirical and behavioural-economics findings across household finance topics.
alternates.why_it_matters: Gives the broad synthesis and vocabulary of choice-architecture and product-design interventions in household finance the brief needs as a review-level reference, spanning beyond the employer-retirement literature to consumer product design generally.
limitations: broad overview rather than a focused effect-size estimate on round-up savings defaults
abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes
alternates.relevance_reason: Serves the portfolio's need for a synthesis/review of the choice-architecture literature across consumer financial products, not only employer retirement plans.
alternates.title: Behavioral Household Finance
alternates.abstract: This chapter provides an overview of household finance. The first part summarizes key facts regarding household financial behavior, emphasizing empirical regularities that are inconsistent with the standard classical economic model and discussing extensions of the classical model and explanations grounded in behavioral economics that can account for the observed patterns. This part covers five topics: consumption and savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance. The second part addresses interventions that firms, governments, and other parties deploy to shape household financial outcomes: education and information, peer effects and social influence, product design, advice and disclosure, choice architecture, and interventions that directly target prices or quantities.

alternates.key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out cost together; adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20-30% menu would capture 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
alternates.methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million transaction records plus an independent stated-preference survey.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly informs the 'level' decision: it models how a preset menu of numeric options anchors chosen amounts and what changing the menu does to welfare versus revenue — the same structural question as choosing which round-up multiplier to preset and whether to add more options.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a savings product
US taxi setting, not an EU banking app
alternates.relevance_reason: Closest available structural analysis of how a preset numeric menu anchors consumer choice and what changing the menu does to welfare, directly transferable to the round-up multiplier design decision.
alternates.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
alternates.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

alternates.key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated browser choice screens, Firefox usage was 113% higher on iOS and 12% higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual, with effects persisting at least 15 months.
alternates.methodology: Difference-in-differences quasi-experiment exploiting the staggered rollout of EU-mandated choice screens across iOS and Android.
alternates.why_it_matters: Provides rare 15-month persistence evidence on a real EU-regulated active-choice intervention altering default-driven behavior at scale, directly informing whether active choice produces durable change rather than a one-off signup blip.
limitations: Mobile browser default setting, not a financial or savings product
Underlying mechanism (search/browser preference) differs from a savings-contribution decision
alternates.relevance_reason: Closest available large-scale, long-horizon evidence on active-choice mandates changing default-driven behavior in the exact EU regulatory context the brief operates in.
alternates.title: The Effect of Choice Screens on Mobile Browser Usage: Evidence from the EU Digital Markets Act
alternates.abstract: Can active choice mitigate the effects of preset defaults? We study this question using a difference-in-differences design around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions. We find large effects, with notable differences across platforms: from 15 months after the mandate onward, Firefox usage was 113 percent higher on iOS and 12 percent higher on Android relative to a no-mandate counterfactual. This gap is consistent with rollout differences, as Android showed choice screens primarily on new devices, whereas iOS also showed them on existing devices.Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.
alternates.tldr: Large effects are found around the rollout of the EU’s Digital Markets Act, which required iOS and Android to display browser choice screens under certain conditions, with notable differences across platforms.
